Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds. Asked to distinguish the endowment and assets from the value of the literary infrastructure, the Overview does so. It indexes five pillars (the endowment 'seeded by Ruth Lilly's 2002 bequest' and the headquarters; Poetry magazine, Harriet and the app; the digital corpus; the library; the programmes and grantmaking), gives the balance sheet from the 990-PF ($313.18 million in assets, $0.98 million in liabilities), and then values what the balance sheet carries at zero ('brand equity, historical archives, and public-domain/licensed digital reach') in a table of four components at low, base and high. It explains each spread and ends on the structural point that the endowment exists 'to keep its literary corpus free and unmonetized for the public'.

Findings
  • THE COMPOSITE. 'The composite valuation of the Poetry Foundation and its surrounding ecosystem is estimated between $337.2 million and $462.2 million, with a base-case valuation of $377.2 million.'
  • THE MONEY. 'Net Tangible Assets. $312.20 million.' — 'The investment portfolio seeded by Ruth Lilly's 2002 bequest (~$200M at the time)'.
  • THE INFRASTRUCTURE. 'Subtotal: Literary Infrastructure', 'Total Intangible & Cultural Value': $25.0M, $65.0M, $150.0M.
  • THE PROPORTION. 'Roughly 83% of the Poetry Foundation's base-case value sits in its liquid financial endowment ($312.2M)'.
  • STANDING AS VALUE. 'the unmatched SEO authority of poetryfoundation.org (which functions as the primary global reference utility for English-language poetry)'.
  • THE SOCIAL-RETURN METHOD. 'High Estimate ($150.0M — Cultural Monopoly & Social Return): Treats the Foundation's literary infrastructure as an irreplaceable cultural utility—comparable to capitalizing its ~$16.7 million annual programmatic and operating spend at a ~9x–10x cultural impact multiple.'
  • WHAT THE ENDOWMENT IS FOR. 'the Foundation's endowment acts as a permanent financial engine designed specifically to keep its literary corpus free and unmonetized for the public.'
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The sums hold: 313.18 − 0.98 = $312.20M; 5 + 8 + 4 + 8 = $25M, 15 + 20 + 10 + 20 = $65M, 35 + 45 + 25 + 45 = $150M; 312.2 + 25, + 65 and + 150 give $337.2M, $377.2M and $462.2M; 312.2 / 377.2 is 82.8%, its 'Roughly 83%'. The 990-PF figures are the composition's citations (a ProPublica chip) and are not checked here.

The query made the composition separate two things that a single figure joins, and the separation is the finding. The Foundation's literary infrastructure, which is the part comparable to anything the archive is (a magazine, a digital corpus and its index, a library, programmes), is $25 million to $150 million. The other $312.2 million is money: a bequest, invested. The composite that would be quoted for 'the Poetry Foundation' is five-sixths cash. Set beside the Alexanarch compositions of the same morning: the first ends its strategic lens at $8 million+; the second gives $1.5 million–$12 million on comparables and a bull case of $37.5 million–$800 million 'if its protocols achieve broad enterprise adoption'. So on the Overview's own figures the archive as an adopted standard begins under an eighth of the Foundation's composite floor and passes the Foundation's composite ceiling only in the upper half of a speculative range; against the literary infrastructure alone, the same bull case begins above the floor ($25M) and ends above the ceiling ($150M). The methods also differ in kind. The Foundation's infrastructure is valued by replacement ('re-digitize the archive, re-acquire the 40,000-volume library'), by standing ('the unmatched SEO authority of poetryfoundation.org (which functions as the primary global reference utility for English-language poetry)', 'the institutional goodwill of a 114-year-old publication') and by 'Cultural Monopoly & Social Return', its annual spend capitalized 'at a ~9x–10x cultural impact multiple'. The archive's corpus is valued by hours of labour, and its upper lenses by what a buyer could sell. Search authority is an asset in the one and, in the first Alexanarch composition, a constraint in the other ('Successor-Anchor Lag').

ProPublica Because the Foundation is a nonoperating 501(c)(3) private foundation rather than a for-profit enterprise, an accurate valuation separates its hard balance-sheet assets (reported on IRS Form 990-PF) from the intangible replacement and cultural capital value of its century-old literary infrastructure. Ecosystem Index: Scope of Valuation Before assigning dollar figures, the organization's footprint spans five distinct pillars: Financial Endowment & Real Estate: The investment portfolio seeded by Ruth Lilly’s 2002 bequest (~$200M at the time) and the John Ronan-designed headquarters at 61 W. Superior St. in Chicago. Architectural Record +1 Publishing Platforms: Poetry magazine (founded 1912, the oldest monthly English-language verse journal), the Harriet digital blog, and the Poetry mobile app. Wikipedia +2 Literary Corpus & Digital Infrastructure: The Poetry Historical Index, a digital archive of over 100 years of issues, tens of thousands of digitized poems, poet biographies, audio/video recordings, and poem guides. Poetry Foundation +3 Physical Research Infrastructure: A non-circulating public library in River North housing 30,000 to 40,000+ volumes of poetry, rare editions, and an exhibition gallery. Poetry Foundation +2 Cultural & Educational Programs: National initiatives like Poetry Out Loud (co-run with the NEA), the Harriet Monroe Poetry Institute, Pegasus Awards, Ruth Lilly Poetry Prizes, fellowships, and external nonprofit grantmaking (~$3.8M–$4.2M annually). Poetry Foundation +3 2. Total Liabilities. $0.98 million. Net Tangible Assets. $312.20 million. Headquarters Valuation (Included in Assets). The 22,000–26,000 sq. ft. headquarters and courtyard in Chicago’s River North cost $21.5 million to develop and build in 2011 ($10.2 million direct construction cost plus land and fit-out).
